subject: physics
title: Series and parallel circuits
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Series and parallel circuits — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.2.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Series and parallel circuits, specification section 4.2.2.
final_note: You worked through Series and parallel circuits — 19 specification statements.

concepts.def: Components are in series when they are joined one after another in a single loop, so there is only one path for charge. Every charge that passes through one component must pass through all the others.
Components are in parallel when they are joined side by side between the same two points, so the charge has a choice of paths. Each component sits on its own branch of the circuit.
A point in a circuit where the conducting path divides or rejoins. Charge that arrives at a junction each second equals the charge that leaves it each second, so no charge is created or lost there.
In series there is the same current through each component, because there is only one path and charge is not used up. Moving an ammeter to a different place in the loop does not change its reading.

concepts.term: Sharing of potential difference in series
concepts.def: The total potential difference of the power supply is shared between components connected in series, so the separate potential differences add up to the supply potential difference.
The total resistance of two components in series is the sum of the resistance of each component, R_total = R_1 + R_2, because the charge has to pass through both in turn.
The potential difference across each component connected in parallel is the same, because the ends of every branch are joined to the same two points in the circuit.

concepts.term: Total current in a parallel circuit
concepts.def: The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components, because the current from the supply divides between the branches and rejoins afterwards.
The total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor, because the second resistor gives the charge an extra path to flow along.
The unit of resistance, R, is the ohm, symbol Ω. A component has a resistance of one ohm when a potential difference of one volt across it drives a current of one ampere through it.
A single resistance that could replace a group of resistors without changing the current drawn from the supply. For resistors in series it is found by adding the individual resistances.
An ammeter measures current and is connected in series with the component whose current is wanted, so that the same current passes through both the meter and that component.
A voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel with the component, that is across its two ends, so it experiences the same potential difference as that component.
A direct current supply, such as a cell or battery, drives charge around the circuit in one direction only. The dc series circuits used for measurement and testing are built from such a supply.
A circuit that contains both series and parallel parts, for example a resistor in series with a pair of lamps that are in parallel with each other.

concepts.term: Variable resistor in a test circuit
concepts.def: A resistor whose resistance can be changed. Placed in series in a test circuit it alters the current, so several pairs of current and potential difference readings can be taken for one component.

mcqs.q: A lamp and a fixed resistor are connected in series with a cell. An ammeter placed between the cell and the lamp reads 0.30 A. A second ammeter is placed between the lamp and the resistor. What does the second ammeter read?
options: Less than 0.30 A, because some of the current is used up inside the lamp
0.15 A, because the current from the cell is shared between the two parts
0.30 A, because in series there is the same current through each of the components
0.30 A, but only if the resistor is placed nearer to the cell than the lamp
mcqs.explain: For components connected in series there is the same current through each component, so both ammeters read 0.30 A.

mcqs.q: A 6 V battery is connected in series with two identical lamps. A voltmeter across the first lamp reads 3 V. What does a voltmeter across the second lamp read?
options: 3 V, because the supply potential difference is shared between the two lamps
6 V, because each component in series has the full supply potential difference
0 V, because the first lamp has already used up the potential difference
3 V, but only if the second lamp is the one nearer to the negative terminal
mcqs.explain: The total potential difference of the power supply is shared between components in series, so the two equal shares are 3 V each.

mcqs.q: A 4 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are joined in series. What is the total resistance of the pair?
options: 2 Ω, found by taking the difference of the two values
5 Ω, the value that lies midway between the two resistors
Under 4 Ω, since joining resistors gives the charge more paths
10 Ω, found by adding the two resistance values together
mcqs.explain: R_total = R_1 + R_2, so the total resistance is 4 Ω + 6 Ω = 10 Ω.

mcqs.q: The specification gives the equation R_total = R_1 + R_2. Which statement does this equation express?
options: The total resistance of two components in parallel is the sum of each resistance
The total resistance of two components in series is the sum of each resistance
The total resistance of two components in series is set by the larger resistor alone
The total resistance of two components in series lies midway between the two values
mcqs.explain: This is the series rule exactly as the specification states it: the total resistance of two components is the sum of the resistance of each component.

mcqs.q: A student is writing a key for a circuit table. Which line gives the quantity, its symbol and its unit for resistance as the specification states them?
options: Resistance, symbol Ω, measured in units called R, put after the value
Resistance, symbol R, measured in volts, whose unit symbol is V
Resistance, symbol I, measured in ohms, whose unit symbol is Ω
Resistance, symbol R, measured in ohms, for which the unit symbol is Ω
mcqs.explain: The specification states: resistance, R, in ohms, Ω.

mcqs.q: Two lamps of different resistances are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. A voltmeter across the first lamp reads 12 V. What does a voltmeter across the second lamp read?
options: 6 V, since the potential difference of the battery is shared between the two branches
Less than 12 V, since the first lamp has taken some potential difference
12 V, since the potential difference across each component in parallel is the same
12 V, but only when both of the lamps have exactly the same resistance
mcqs.explain: Both branches are joined between the same two points, so each has the full 12 V across it.

mcqs.q: In a parallel circuit one branch carries a current of 0.40 A and the other carries 0.25 A. What is the current in the wire leading from the supply?
options: 0.65 A, the sum of the currents in the two branches
0.40 A, the same as the current within the larger branch
0.15 A, found from the difference of the branch values
0.325 A, the average of the two branch currents
mcqs.explain: The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components.

mcqs.q: A 20 Ω resistor and a 5 Ω resistor are joined in parallel. Which statement about the total resistance of this pair is correct?
options: It is 25 Ω, the two resistance values added together
It is below 5 Ω, the smaller of the two resistances
It is 12.5 Ω, halfway between the two resistance values
It is between 5 Ω and 20 Ω, but closer to the 5 Ω one
mcqs.explain: The total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor.

mcqs.q: Explain why connecting a second resistor in series with the first increases the total resistance of the circuit.
options: The charge now has to pass through both resistors in turn, so the single path opposes it more
The second resistor gives the charge another path to follow, and each path opposes it
The second resistor uses up part of the current before it reaches the first resistor
The supply now has to share its potential difference, so it pushes the charge less hard
mcqs.explain: In series the one path is effectively made harder to get through, so the resistances add and the total rises.

mcqs.q: Explain why connecting a second resistor in parallel with the first decreases the total resistance of the circuit.
options: The two resistance values simply add, and the supply is shared between the branches
The total has to lie between the two values, so it falls below the larger
The second resistor adds another path, so more charge can flow for the same supply
Each of the resistors now carries only half the current, so each opposes it less
mcqs.explain: An extra route for charge means a larger total current for the same potential difference, which is a smaller total resistance.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes a difference between series circuits and parallel circuits?
options: In series the potential difference is the same across each component; in parallel the current is
In series the components share out the current; in parallel they share the potential difference
In series there is one path for charge; in parallel each branch carries equal current
In series the current is the same in each component; in parallel the potential difference is
mcqs.explain: This states both rules the specification gives: same current through each series component, same potential difference across each parallel component.

mcqs.q: A student wants to measure the current in a lamp and the potential difference across it. How should the two meters be connected?
options: Ammeter in parallel with the lamp, voltmeter in series with it
Ammeter in series with the lamp, voltmeter across its ends
Both of the meters in series with the lamp, one on each side
Both of the meters in parallel with the lamp, across its ends
mcqs.explain: The ammeter must carry the lamp's current, so it goes in series; the voltmeter must span the lamp's ends, so it goes in parallel.

mcqs.q: A dc series circuit for testing a component contains a cell, an ammeter, a variable resistor and the component, with a voltmeter across the component. Why is the variable resistor included?
options: It keeps the current steady while the potential difference across the component is varied
It makes the current the same in every part of the circuit while the test is carried out
It protects the voltmeter by taking a share of the current passing the meter
It changes the current, so several pairs of readings can be taken for the component under test
mcqs.explain: Altering its resistance alters the total resistance of the series loop, and so the current, giving a range of readings.

mcqs.q: A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 3 Ω resistor and a 5 Ω resistor. What is the current in the circuit?
options: 1.5 A, from 12 V divided by the total resistance of 8 Ω
4 A, from 12 V divided by the 3 Ω resistor on its own
6 A, from 12 V divided by the 2 Ω difference of the pair
2.4 A, from 12 V divided by the 5 Ω resistor by itself
mcqs.explain: The series resistances add to 8 Ω, and 12 V ÷ 8 Ω = 1.5 A, the same current through both resistors.

mcqs.q: A 9 V supply is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor?
options: 9 V, as each component has the whole supply across it
4.5 V, as the supply is shared equally between them
6 V, from the 1.5 A current in the 4 Ω resistor
3 V, an equal share among the three parts
mcqs.explain: Total resistance 6 Ω gives a current of 1.5 A, and 1.5 A × 4 Ω = 6 V across the larger resistor.

mcqs.q: Three 6 Ω resistors are connected in series across a 9 V supply. Using the idea of equivalent resistance, what current does the supply deliver?
options: 1.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of 6 Ω alone
0.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of 18 Ω
3 A, using an equivalent resistance of just 3 Ω
4.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of just 2 Ω
mcqs.explain: The three series resistances add to an equivalent 18 Ω, and 9 V ÷ 18 Ω = 0.5 A.

mcqs.q: In a circuit a cell is joined to a resistor, and the resistor is joined to two lamps that are placed side by side between the same pair of junctions. How is this circuit best described?
options: It has both kinds of part: the resistor is in series with a parallel pair of lamps
It is a series circuit, because all of the components are joined to one cell
It is a parallel circuit, because the circuit contains more than one branch
It is neither, because a circuit has to be all series or all parallel
mcqs.explain: Some circuits include both series and parallel parts, and this is one of them.

mcqs.q: Three lamps are connected in series with a cell. One lamp is taken out of its holder. What happens to the other two lamps?
options: They both stay lit, because each lamp has its own path back to the cell
They both stay lit but shine brighter, as the total resistance falls
They both go out, because the single path round the circuit has been broken
The lamp before the empty holder stays lit, but the lamp after it goes out
mcqs.explain: In series there is only one path, so removing any component stops the current everywhere in the loop.

mcqs.q: Two lamps are connected in parallel across a cell. One of the lamps is taken out of its holder. What happens to the remaining lamp?
options: It goes out, since taking one lamp out breaks the circuit
It stays lit as before, since its own branch is still complete
It shines more brightly, since it now receives all of the current
It shines more dimly, since the supply now delivers less current
mcqs.explain: The remaining branch still has the full supply potential difference across it, so its current is unchanged.

mcqs.q: A circuit diagram shows a cell, a closed switch and two lamps drawn side by side between the same two junctions. Which measurement would best check that the built circuit matches the diagram?
options: Check that exactly the same current passes through each of the lamps
Check that the two lamp potential differences add up to the supply value
Check that the pair has a larger resistance than either lamp on its own
Check that each lamp has the full supply potential difference on it
mcqs.explain: Equal potential difference across each component, equal to the supply, is the test for a parallel connection.

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.2.2 Series and parallel circuits
